Chapter 4: Addressing Specific Needs—Praying Through Life’s Stages and Challenges
You know, as kids grow up, their needs and the challenges they face are always changing. One thing this book really highlights is how important it is to adapt our prayers—so they actually fit what our kids are going through at each stage of life. After all, what a toddler needs is worlds apart from what a teenager or a young adult might be wrestling with. So, prayer isn’t one-size-fits-all; it’s something we can shape to meet those shifting realities.
Let’s start with early childhood. These first years are when little ones are starting to understand the world for the very first time. In this stage, our prayers often center on safety, healthy growth, and building those first blocks of character—things like kindness, curiosity, and learning to listen. Maybe you find yourself praying for protection from accidents, for peaceful sleep at night, or simply for your child to discover and enjoy learning.
Then comes the school-age years. Suddenly, there’s homework, new friendships, and all sorts of new experiences. School can bring a whole set of pressures—like how to handle tricky subjects, deal with peer pressure, or make good choices. Here, prayers might focus on helping your child navigate friendships, find confidence, or even stand up to bullying. You might ask for them to be surrounded by positive influences, or for wisdom when they’re facing tough decisions.
Now, let’s talk about adolescence. The teenage years can be a wild ride—there’s more independence, lots of questions about identity, and sometimes a little bit of rebellion in the mix. In this season, prayers often become about guidance and self-control, and the courage to resist negative influences. Maybe you’re praying for open conversations, for your teen to find their sense of purpose, or the strength to stick to their values when it’s not easy.
And then there’s young adulthood. As kids become adults, their focus shifts to big decisions—careers, relationships, and what their faith means to them personally. Here, prayers might be about discernment, healthy relationships, and finding a sense of calling. You may find yourself asking for wisdom as they take on new responsibilities, or for them to stay connected to their spiritual roots as they branch out into the world.
No matter the stage, there are a few things the book encourages parents to always keep in mind:
First, stay attuned to their changing needs. Check in regularly—what’s happening in your child’s life right now? Adjust your prayers so they really reflect what’s going on.
Second, pray for character development. Sure, immediate needs are important. But don’t forget to pray for the long-term stuff—like honesty, compassion, and perseverance.
And third, intercede for their relationships. Because family, friends, teachers, and mentors have such a huge impact, praying for those connections can make all the difference in how a child grows.
Imagine you’re the parent of a teenager who’s really struggling with self-image or fitting in. Instead of just worrying or offering advice, you can pray for your child to see themselves the way God sees them—to find friends who really support them, and to build resilience when criticism comes their way.
This stage-specific approach to prayer is practical, but it’s also deeply compassionate. It recognizes that kids are always changing, and that being a good parent means staying flexible, paying close attention, and being willing to seek guidance for each new challenge along the way.
